items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Work : A Multidimensional Framework for Assessing Technological Exposure, Adoption, and Employment Impacts
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are transforming the productive core of the global economy, yet public debate remains dominated by single-number claims about the proportion of jobs “at risk”—claims that collapse heterogeneous technologies, tasks, and adoption conditions into a single misleading index. This thesis develops, verifies, and applies a multidimensional framework for assessing the employment consequences of AI and automation across economic sectors. The framework distinguishes four constructs that previous research has often conflated: (D1) digital AI exposure, defined as the proportion of a sector’s task content that current AI systems can technically support or perform; (D2) physical automation, defined as the automatable share of embodied, manual tasks; (D3) adoption, defined as the actual, observed deployment of AI and automation technologies within a sector; and (D4) net employment impact, defined as the estimated medium-term effect on total employment after accounting for displacement, reinstatement, and the creation of new tasks. The thesis proceeds in four stages. First, it reconstructs the technical foundations of machine learning, generative models, and robotics with sufficient rigor for economic analysis, while tracing the economic theory of technology-induced labor reallocation from Ricardo’s machinery question to the contemporary task-based literature. Second, it formalizes the four-dimensional framework through explicit index definitions, aggregation functions, and uncertainty treatment, deriving each dimension from documented methodologies, including task-exposure assessments, adoption surveys, and causal labor-market studies. Third, it applies the framework to nine sectors: information technology, finance and insurance, healthcare, education, manufacturing, construction, transportation and logistics, hospitality and food services, and retail and e-commerce. This analysis synthesizes approximately 280 verified sources, including causal evidence on industrial robots, randomized evaluations of generative AI assistants, and institutional data on technology adoption. Fourth, it examines the implications of the findings, demonstrating that sector-level net employment effects are mediated more strongly by adoption frictions, complementarities, and institutional conditions than by raw technical exposure alone. Employment effects are distributed unevenly across sectors and occupations rather than being confined to aggregate outcomes, and policy interventions can influence outcomes along all four dimensions. Methodologically, the thesis is grounded in a systematic review protocol with preregistered inclusion criteria, a two-pass, point-by-point verification of every citation, reference, and internal cross-reference, and an automated consistency audit whose results are reported in full. Its central conclusion is that a one-size-fits-all approach is inadequate: accurately assessing the labor-market consequences of AI requires keeping the four dimensions analytically distinct, because technologies with identical exposure profiles can produce opposing employment outcomes under different adoption conditions and institutional arrangements. The thesis concludes with scenario analyses for 2035 and a policy agenda addressing education, social protection, taxation, competition, and AI governance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in the Food Industry: Transforming Food Quality, Production, and Sustainable Food Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the food industry by enabling data driven approaches to food quality assessment, safety management, product development, processing, packaging, storage, and supply chain operations. The growing availability of data from sensors, imaging systems, analytical instruments, and digital production platforms has created new opportunities for machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and predictive analytics across the food chain. This chapter reviews the current applications of these technologies in food systems, with particular emphasis on quality and safety assessment, formulation and product development, process optimization, intelligent packaging, shelf life prediction, logistics, and supply chain management. The potential contribution of AI to sustainable food systems is also discussed, including food loss and waste reduction, resource optimization, and circular food production. In addition, emerging applications of generative AI are examined in areas such as food innovation, sensory and consumer research, and research support. Despite these opportunities, challenges related to data quality, model validation, interpretability, privacy, infrastructure, and human oversight remain important considerations. Overall, AI has considerable potential to support more efficient, responsive, and sustainable food systems when computational approaches are integrated with food science expertise and appropriate experimental validation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Digital Image Forgery Detection
items.abstract: With the growing use of digital images in online communication and social media, verifying whether an image is authentic has become increasingly important. Image manipulation techniques such as copy-move, splicing, inpainting, and object removal can change the meaning of visual information. At the same time, JPEG compression and repeated recompression can weaken the forensic traces that are useful for detection. This review looks at two AI-based approaches for detecting digital image forgery. The first study combines Error Level Analysis (ELA) with the VGG-16 convolutional neural network to classify images as original or tampered. The second study focuses on compressed images shared through social networks and uses a modified ShuffleNet V2 architecture for lightweight forgery classification. The two studies are reviewed based on their objectives, datasets, preprocessing or feature representation, deep learning architecture, compression conditions, findings, and limitations. The comparison shows that ELA with VGG-16 can help expose compression-related manipulation artifacts, while the modified ShuffleNet V2 approach focuses on the practical challenge of detecting forgery after JPEG and social-network recompression. The review highlights dataset diversity, compression robustness, computational efficiency, and generalization across different manipulation and sharing conditions as important research gaps. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Image Forgery, Deep Learning, Error Level Analysis, VGG-16,ShuffleNet V2, Image Compression.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as academic infrastructure: governance, administrative intelligence, and AI fluency in Kazakhstan’s higher education sector
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly part of higher education's institutional infrastructure, extending beyond teaching and learning to governance, administration, and student support. This study examines how AI Governance Readiness (AIGR) influences Administrative Efficiency through AI (AEAI), AI Fluency Orientation (AIFO), and Student Retention Intentions (SRI), while assessing the mediating roles of AEAI and AIFO and the moderating role of Equity Perception (EPS) in Kazakhstan's higher education sector. Drawing on Dynamic Capability Theory and Sociotechnical Systems Theory, the study develops and empirically tests an institutional capability model using 935 valid responses from students, faculty, academic administrators, and digital administration staff across public and private universities. The scholars analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.0, supported by RStudio. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, while the structural model showed adequate explanatory and predictive performance. We assessed common method bias through procedural safeguards and full-collinearity diagnostics, and identified no substantive concerns. The findings show that AIGR is positively associated with AEAI and AIFO, while both constructs positively influence SRI. AEAI and AIFO also significantly mediate the relationship between AIGR and SRI. However, EPS does not significantly moderate the relationships between AI-enabled institutional capabilities and retention intentions. The findings position AI governance as a strategic institutional capability through which universities can improve administrative responsiveness, develop AI-related competencies, and support student continuity. The study contributes empirical evidence from Kazakhstan to the growing literature on responsible AI governance and digital transformation in higher education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence empowered NB-IoT systems: architectures, advances, and future perspectives
items.abstract: Abstract With an increasing number of devices being installed in agriculture, factories, hospitals, and cities, the need for intelligent, trustworthy, and energy-efficient communication systems is rising. This is one such system: Narrow Band Internet of Things, or NB-IoT, which connects devices at a long range with low-power consumption. But it also has a poor reaction time and is not adaptable to changing situations. This review discusses how artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), deep learning, and other intelligent methods, are making NB-IoT more adaptable and predictive. By deploying lightweight AI models and edge computing—that is, processing locally on a device—systems are able to better manage wireless signals, save battery life, and improve overall performance. It also discusses several related real-world applications in the area of agriculture, healthcare, industry, and smart cities and achieves benefits such as saving water, early disease diagnosis, predictive machine maintenance, and environmental monitoring. The integration of AI with NB-IoT fosters digital solutions toward sustainability, security, and being human-centric. All the progress made thus far will be of immense utility to decision-makers, engineers, planners of smart cities, and service providers who look to smarter, more affordable, privacy-friendly technology for the future.

items.title: Artificial intelligence ethical awareness and academic integrity among medical students at the University of Khartoum: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare and medical education implies significant opportunities along with significant ethical challenges. Despite the substantial medical student uptake of artificial intelligence globally, little comprehensive assessments of ethical awareness are being conducted. This study aimed to assess artificial intelligence awareness and academic integrity level among University of Khartoum medical students and to examine relationships between the awareness level, demographic factors, artificial intelligence exposure, and tool use behavior. An institutional cross-sectional descriptive study of Years 3–6 medical students at University of Khartoum Faculty of Medicine in 2025 was conducted. A convenience sampling with quota allocation was used, and 349 students responded. The instrument included demographic variables, artificial intelligence exposure measures, and the 32-item Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity Scale. Nonparametric tests were applied. Participants were predominantly female (69.3%) with a mean age of 22.85 years. The median total Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity score was 4.16, indicative of moderate ethical awareness based on sample-derived empirical tertiles. Privacy and Data Protection were highest (median 4.67), with lowest scores in Transparency and Fairness/Non-Discrimination (3.80). Female students were more aware ( P = .01). No year-based differences observed. While 63.9% had minimal formal artificial intelligence exposure, 51.6% had moderate to high informal exposure. ChatGPT usage was prevalent (94.6%), and Google Gemini/Notebook LM usage was strongly associated with higher awareness ( P = .003). Informal exposure was positively correlated with awareness ( P = .01), but formal exposure was not. Multiple regression indicated that gender, informal exposure, and tool accounted for 11.2% of the variance in awareness. University of Khartoum medical students showed moderate-to-high aggregate artificial intelligence, ethical sensitivity, with areas of privacy protection and accountability being of particular strength. Gaps exist for awareness of transparency and fairness. The dominance of informal learning pathways over formal instruction, and gender variability favoring female students are significant findings. Findings highlight the need for institutional policies and conducting longitudinal research to track the evolution of AI ethics throughout medical training.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Sustainability and Climate Change Mitigation: Recent Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Abstract Climate change and environmental degradation have emerged as two of the most pressing global challenges of the twenty-first century, threatening ecosystems, biodiversity, human health, and sustainable development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed environmental research and management by enabling advanced data analytics, real-time monitoring, predictive modeling, and intelligent decision-support systems. This review critically examines the applications of AI in addressing environmental and climate-related challenges, including climate forecasting, air and water quality monitoring, biodiversity conservation, precision agriculture, renewable energy optimization, carbon emission assessment, waste management, and disaster risk reduction. Furthermore, The review also identifies current research gaps and highlights future opportunities for developing transparent, energy-efficient, and explainable AI systems that support evidence-based environmental decisionmaking. It concludes that AI has become a transformative tool for accelerating progress toward climate change mitigation, environmental sustainability, and the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, and policy support will be essential to maximize the environmental benefits of AI while minimizing its ecological footprint. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Climate Change; Environmental Sustainability; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Remote Sensing; Internet of Things; Renewable Energy; Biodiversity Conservation; Sustainable Development Goals.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for medication recognition and safety: a systematic review of detection, classification, OCR, and digital health applications
items.abstract: Introduction Medication errors and adverse drug events remain causes of patient harm, underscoring the need for technologies supporting medication identification, verification, and medication safety. Artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, optical character recognition (OCR), and digital health technologies are applied to medication recognition. Objective To systematically review AI-based medication recognition systems and characterize recognition tasks, computational approaches, datasets, evaluation, validation, generalizability, deployment, applications, and emerging directions. Methods A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and PubMed/MEDLINE were searched for publications from 1 January 2016 to 4 September 2026, using two conceptual blocks covering medication recognition and AI methods. Of 895 retrieved records, 136 duplicates were removed, and 759 records underwent screening. After full-text assessment, 14 reports were excluded, and 91 studies were included. Title-and-abstract screening yielded 84.72% observed agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.527 ). For methodological assessment, both reviewers independently applied D1–D8 to the 91 included studies before consensus resolution. Across 728 domain-level assessments, observed agreement was 97.66%, with an aggregate Cohen’s κ of 0.959; domain-specific κ values ranged from 0.857 to 1.000. Evidence was synthesized through cross-study analysis and four evidence maps. Results Evidence shows use of detection, classification, OCR/imprint recognition, hybrid and multimodal architectures, alongside few-shot, low-shot, zero-shot, and incremental learning. Applications extend to assistive, mobile, and IoT-enabled systems, medication verification, and clinical decision support. Heterogeneity in datasets, imaging conditions, evaluation protocols, and validation strategies limits comparison and generalizability. External validation, cross-dataset testing, unseen-medication evaluation, prospective deployment, and clinical testing remain limited. Conclusion AI-based medication recognition is evolving from a computer vision task into a digital informatics component supporting medication safety, accessibility, verification, and patient care. Future research should prioritize diverse datasets, leakage control, independent multicenter validation, unseen-medication evaluation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, interoperability, and resource-efficient deployment. Evaluation should extend beyond accuracy to clinical utility, safety, usability, trust, and patient-centered outcomes.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Net-Zero and Climate-Resilient Sustainable Cities: Technologies, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Urbanization, climate change, increasing energy demand, and rapid infrastructure development have created significant challenges for achieving sustainable and resilient cities. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology that enables data-driven decision-making, intelligent automation, and efficient resource management, making it an important enabler of net-zero and climate-resilient urban systems. This narrative review examines AI applications relevant to urban climate mitigation and adaptation, drawing on literature identified through Google Scholar and ScienceDirect. The review examines the role of machine learning, deep learning, Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, cloud computing, digital twins, and generative AI in improving urban energy systems, sustainable transportation, environmental monitoring, infrastructure management, and smart governance. The study also discusses how these technologies contribute to carbon emission reduction, renewable energy integration, climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, and efficient urban planning. In addition, major challenges associated with AI implementation are critically analyzed, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, lack of interoperability, high energy consumption of AI systems, digital inequality, and governance issues. Emerging research trends such as explainable AI, green AI, AI-enabled digital twins, federated learning, and human-centered smart governance are highlighted as important directions for future research. Based on the reviewed literature, the study proposes future research priorities that emphasize interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, standardized urban data frameworks, and sustainable policy development. Overall, AI has the potential to accelerate the transition toward intelligent, low-carbon, and climate-resilient cities. The synthesis is qualitative and non-exhaustive, with limitations arising from unavailable original search and screening records and differences between study settings and outcome measures. However, the successful implementation of AI will depend on integrating technological innovation with ethical governance, public participation, and long-term sustainability planning to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ACADEMIC WRITING: OPPORTUNITIES, CHALLENGES, AND ETHICAL GUIDELINES FOR HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed academic writing, creating new opportunities for students, researchers, and university teachers. AI-powered applications can assist users in generating ideas, organizing arguments, improving grammar, expanding vocabulary, paraphrasing sentences, and editing academic texts. However, the integration of these technologies into higher education also raises important questions concerning academic integrity, authorship, originality, critical thinking, and the reliability of automatically generated information. This article examines the role of AI in academic writing, focusing on its educational benefits, methodological limitations, and ethical implications. The study employs a qualitative, descriptive-analytical approach based on a review of relevant academic literature and international guidelines on generative AI in education and research. The analysis suggests that AI can support the development of academic writing when it is used as an assistive instrument rather than a substitute for independent intellectual work. Particular attention is paid to the responsibilities of students, researchers, and educational institutions in ensuring transparent and responsible AI use. The article argues that effective integration requires AI literacy, critical evaluation of generated content, appropriate disclosure practices, and assessment methods that recognize the importance of human reasoning. It concludes that the educational value of AI depends not simply on technological availability but on the principles governing its application in academic contexts.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Alternative, Nonformal, and Adult Learning in the Global South: Protocol for a Mixed-Methods Systematic Review
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education has expanded rapidly, yet it remains concentrated in higher education and formal schooling in high-income countries. Alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs, which serve out-of-school youth and adults across the Global South, are largely absent from this evidence base. No systematic synthesis has examined how AI is used in these programs, what outcomes it produces, and what conditions shape its adoption. Objective: This protocol describes a mixed-methods systematic review that will identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on AI use in alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Methods: The review follows the JBI methodology for mixed-methods systematic reviews and is reported according to PRISMA-P. Searches will cover Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, four regional databases, and grey literature sources for studies published from January 2015 onward. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and appraise quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Quantitative findings will be synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline, with meta-analysis where at least three comparable studies exist. Qualitative findings will be synthesized thematically. Both strands will be integrated through a convergent segregated approach, and certainty of evidence will be rated with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual. Discussion: The review will provide the first consolidated synthesis of AI use in second-chance and adult learning in the Global South. Its findings will inform program managers, teacher developers, and policymakers responsible for programs such as the Philippine Alternative Learning System (ALS). Keywords: artificial intelligence; generative AI; nonformal education; adult learning; Alternative Learning System; Global South; systematic review protocol

items.title: Artificial intelligence in health insurance fraud detection: a global and regional systematic review
items.abstract: Health insurance fraud imposes substantial financial burdens on healthcare systems and reduces the efficiency of healthcare resource utilization worldwide. Traditional fraud detection approaches often struggle to analyse large and complex healthcare claims data, making artificial intelligence (AI) an increasingly important tool for identifying fraudulent activities. This study systematically reviews global and regional evidence on AI applications in health insurance fraud detection, with particular emphasis on methodological approaches, performance evaluation, and implementation challenges. This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Seven electronic databases were searched for studies published between 2016 and 2025. Titles and abstracts were screened using the Silvi AI platform, followed by eligibility assessment according to pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted using a standardized framework, and methodological quality was assessed using the Drummond 10-item checklist. From 450 identified records, 33 studies met the eligibility criteria. The included studies demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in datasets, AI methodologies, fraud types, and performance evaluation metrics. Machine learning was the most frequently applied approach, followed by deep learning, graph-based learning, and hybrid AI frameworks. Although AI-based methods consistently improved fraud detection performance, challenges related to dataset imbalance, standardized reporting, interpretability, external validation, and economic evaluation remain significant barriers to widespread implementation. AI demonstrates considerable potential for improving health insurance fraud detection. However, future research should prioritize standardized evaluation frameworks, explainable AI, external validation across diverse healthcare systems, and economic assessment to support the responsible and scalable deployment of AI-enabled fraud detection systems.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HEALTHCARE: ITS POTENTIALS AND RISKS
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from science fiction into the clinic with remarkable speed. Machine learning systems now read medical scans, flag sepsis before symptoms declare themselves, draft clinical notes, and coach patients through their smartphones. This article examines the promise and the peril of this transformation in narrative form, and then applies the lens to a single, vivid case: the intertwined epidemics of sleep deprivation and migraine in young adults, where wearable sensors and predictive algorithms are beginning to change how these conditions are detected, studied, and managed. The evidence suggests that AI's greatest near-term contribution is not replacing clinicians but extending their reach — while its greatest dangers, including algorithmic bias, opaque decision making, data privacy erosion, and over-reliance, demand deliberate governance. The article argues that the future of medical AI will be decided less by the sophistication of the algorithms than by the wisdom of the humans who deploy them.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review
items.abstract: Background Imaging-guided interventional radiotherapy (IG-IRT) is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer but remains time-consuming and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to improve efficiency and reproducibility. Methods A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2010 and 2026 investigating AI-based imaging applications in cervical IRT. Eligible studies included original research evaluating segmentation (targets and organ at risk), planning, reconstruction, image registration and applicator selection. Results Fifty-two studies were included. Deep learning–based segmentation showed variable performance across anatomical structures and studies, with Dice coefficients approaching or exceeding 0.90 for some organs at risk and target volumes in the best-performing models. Individual studies reported shorter processing times, reduced contouring variability, accurate applicator reconstruction, and potential support for applicator selection. However, the substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity precluded direct comparisons among AI approaches. Conclusions The available studies suggest that AI may support the automation of selected workflow steps and assist treatment-related decision-making in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. While several applications have achieved high technical performance, most remain at the proof-of-concept stage, and robust external validation and prospective clinical evaluation are needed before routine clinical adoption.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in immovable cultural heritage research: a bibliometric and knowledge mapping review
items.abstract: Abstract In recent years, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in immovable cultural heritage research has expanded rapidly, supporting new approaches to heritage documentation, condition assessment, conservation, management, and public communication. In this study, immovable cultural heritage primarily refers to historic buildings, archaeological sites, monuments, cultural landscapes, and other heritage places with fixed spatial locations. Movable cultural objects, museum collections, and intangible cultural heritage are not systematically examined unless the relevant studies directly address the documentation, monitoring, restoration, conservation, or management of immovable heritage. Despite the growing volume of research, existing studies have largely focused on individual technical applications, while comprehensive bibliometric analyses and knowledge-structure mapping from a global perspective remain limited. To address this gap, this study retrieved 382 English-language publications from the Web of Science Core Collection covering the period from 1 January 2015 to 1 October 2025. Using bibliometric methods and analytical tools including VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and ArcGIS, the study examines publication trends, geographical distribution, disciplinary categories, major authors, institutional affiliations, collaboration networks, thematic evolution, and emerging research topics. The results show that publication output increased substantially after 2020. China, Italy, and Spain were among the most productive countries and occupied important positions in the international collaboration network. Major research themes included digital heritage, structural health monitoring, virtual reconstruction, deep learning, remote sensing, and sustainability-related applications. These findings indicate that AI-related research on immovable cultural heritage is strongly represented in engineering, conservation science, computer science, remote sensing, and related technical fields. However, this pattern should not be interpreted as evidence of a general disciplinary shift across cultural heritage studies as a whole. Rather, it reflects the technological orientation of the literature captured by the present search strategy, which was limited to English-language publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection. This study maps the development and knowledge structure of AI applications in immovable cultural heritage research and provides quantitative evidence for identifying major research areas, collaboration patterns, methodological tendencies, and future research needs.

items.abstract: Technological innovation has rarely entered human society without resistance.Some of the concerns that accompanied technologies now regarded as indispensable may appear almost incomprehensible today, although they were taken very seriously at the time.The Industrial Revolution provides perhaps the best-known example.In early nineteenth-century England, the Luddites destroyed textile machinery that they perceived as threatening their jobs, skills, and livelihoods.Their reaction was not simply an irrational fear of machines: it also reflected legitimate concerns about profound changes in working conditions and the distribution of the benefits of technological progress.Nevertheless, mechanization continued and eventually transformed manufacturing and society.Other innovations followed similar paths.Railways were initially regarded by some as potentially dangerous to human health.The automobile encountered resistance and restrictive legislation: the British Locomotive Act of 1865 famously required, under certain circumstances, a person carrying a red flag to precede a self-propelled vehicle.Electricity, elevators, vaccination and, much more recently, the Internet all encountered scepticism, resistance or fear before becoming part of everyday life.History does not teach us that every technological innovation is necessarily beneficial.There have been technologies whose harmful consequences became apparent only after widespread adoption.Nor should legitimate concerns about technological change be dismissed as another form of Luddism.History does, however, suggest that genuinely useful technologies tend eventually to become incorporated into ordinary life and professional practice.Artificial intelligence (AI), and particularly generative AI based on large language models (LLMs), appears likely to follow this pattern.The scientific community is now debating whether and how AI should be used in research, scientific writing, peer review and editorial decision-making.Positions range from enthusiasm to considerable concern.Both attitudes are understandable.AI systems can perform tasks that only a few years ago would have seemed extraordinary.At the same time, their limitations-including inaccurate information, fabricated references, bias, lack of transparency and the generation of extremely convincing but incorrect statements-are equally real [1][2][3][4].The question, therefore, should probably no longer be whether scientists will use AI.They already do, and its use will almost certainly increase.A more useful question is: what should we allow AI to do for us, and what must we never delegate to it? Assistance and Delegation Are Not the Same ThingThis distinction, in our view, is fundamental.AI can be an extraordinarily useful scientific assistant.Consider the preparation of a manuscript.AI can identify grammatical and spelling errors, improve the readability of English, suggest more concise formulations, identify repetitions, detect inconsistencies between different sections of a manuscript and help organize complex material.It can assist in searching the literature and in identifying potentially relevant references, provided that these references are subsequently checked against the original sources.

The discussion highlights how AI strengthens instructional leadership and curriculum fidelity through real-time data insights while addressing critical issues of ethics, governance, and digital equity. items.title: Artificial intelligence maturity in buyer–seller exchange
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping business-to-business (B2B) buying and selling, yet research has largely examined AI as a unilateral process enabler. While this perspective has generated important insights regarding AI adoption and performance, it overlooks a fundamental characteristic of B2B selling: exchange outcomes depend on the compatibility of buyer–seller decision processes at the exchange interface. To address this gap, the authors advance the concept of AI exchange maturity (i.e. extent to which decision authority within buyer–seller exchange is delegated to AI systems) and theorize its organizational antecedents. Building on this construct, the authors develop a bilateral theory of buyer–seller AI exchange in which value co-creation depends on the configuration of AI exchange maturity across exchange partners. The framework identifies four configurations (buyer AI-maturity advantage, seller AI-maturity advantage, agentic-AI maturity alignment, and pre-AI maturity alignment) and theorizes how each configuration shapes value co-creation through information-processing fit and buyer–seller trust. The authors further identify strategies for selling organizations to manage each configuration to enhance value co-creation. In doing so, the framework shifts the theoretical focus from whether individual firms adopt AI to the distribution of decision authority between humans and AI systems across exchange partners.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Related Sentiments and Perceptions on Federated Social Networks: A Computational Text Analysis
items.abstract: This study aims to examine public perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) on federated social networks, specifically Bluesky and Mastodon. While existing research focuses on centralized platforms, a significant gap exists regarding AI perception within decentralized networks. This study addresses this gap through computational analysis of AI related posts in Bluesky and Mastodon. A text-as-data approach was employed to analyze 61,285 posts collected from Bluesky and Mastodon between January 1, 2023, and January 1, 2025. The methodology integrated topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and text analysis to identify prevalent themes, sentiment polarity, and discussion patterns within AI-related discourse. Findings demonstrate predominantly positive sentiment towards AI across both platforms, with trust, anticipation, and joy as primary emotional responses, accompanied by underlying fear and anxiety. Platform-specific variations emerged: Mastodon discourse centers on creativity, digital art, and societal-ethical implications including regulation, bias, and disinformation concerns. Conversely, Bluesky posts emphasize economic and geopolitical dimensions, featuring startups, funding, stock markets, and international policy. The analysis reveals significant fragmentation in public AI perception, characterized by discourse division into distinct economic and ethical spheres across platforms. While this fragmentation accommodates diverse social group perspectives, it presents challenges for establishing comprehensive societal consensus on AI governance. The analytical framework provides insights for understanding decentralized social network dynamics and implications for policy makers examining AI perception in federated digital environments.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Biomarker Discovery in Clinical Biochemistry: Emerging Biomarkers, Machine Learning and Barriers to Clinical Translation
items.abstract: Clinical biochemistry now produces large, multidimensional datasets from automated analysers, laboratory information systems, mass spectrometry and molecular assays. Artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) in particular, offers tools to combine such measurements into multivariable patterns, to monitor laboratory quality and to prioritise candidate biomarkers. This review examines how AI is used across the pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical phases of laboratory work and how it is being applied to four groups of emerging biomarkers: pentraxin-3, extracellular vesicle cargo, circulating microRNAs and adipokines. It describes the main learning approaches, the discovery pipeline, the failure modes that most often inflate reported accuracy (overfitting, data leakage, batch effects and confounding) and a staged validation pathway running from analytical validation to post-deployment monitoring. The literature indicates that AI is most defensible where it supports established laboratory processes and combines established tests with emerging markers. High discrimination in a development cohort does not establish biological validity or clinical usefulness. Standardised measurement, leakage-free modelling, calibration, external and prospective validation, transparent reporting and human oversight are the conditions under which AI-assisted biomarker research can move into routine practice, including in resource-variable settings such as India.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Promising Tool for Cardiovascular Diseases
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) has become a life-threatening condition in recent times. To optimize outcomes in cardiology, artificial intelligence (AI) shows promising potential in diagnosis and, in turn, in the effective prevention of disease. The development of AI has paved the way for significant technological advancements. AI-based systems have improved our understanding of congenital heart disease and various phenotypes of heart failure. This review article focuses on the applications of different types of learning models and neural networks in medicine, diagnosis, and therapy, and highlights how these tools can aid physicians in clinical practice. Although limitations exist in the use of AI-based methods, AI is revolutionizing healthcare practices and holds enormous scope in this field.

items.title: Assessing the ability of a stretched‐grid deep‐learning weather prediction model to capture physical balances
items.abstract: Abstract Weather forecasting has traditionally relied on numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, which simulate weather by solving the governing fluid equations. Recently, the emergence of deep learning weather prediction (DLWP) models has opened a new era in weather forecasting, offering a data‐driven alternative to classical NWP approaches. Regional DLWP models, such as the stretched‐grid model Bris developed by Met Norway, have demonstrated performance on par with or even slightly better than regional NWP models across a range of standard forecast metrics. By overcoming the coarse horizontal resolution that constrained earlier global data‐driven models, the operational use of regional DLWP systems now appears increasingly promising. Nevertheless, the performance of such models during extreme events is generally inferior to that of regional NWP models, and comprehensive evaluations of their ability to generate physically realistic forecasts are still lacking. Here, we present a study comparing the physical consistency of the deterministic version of Bris with the control run of the operational MetCoOp Ensemble Prediction System (MEPS) in forecasting the severe extratropical cyclone Poly , which hit the Netherlands on July 5, 2023. We examine whether Bris represents deviations from key atmospheric balances accurately and whether it reproduces the expected dynamics of the storm. We show that, despite its relatively good performance in terms of root mean square error, Bris struggles to capture important mesoscale features of the event and disrupts several atmospheric balances significantly. This unrealistic disruption is linked mainly to the fine‐scale noise evidenced in its output fields, which leads to incorrect and unrealistic spatial gradients. These results raise critical questions about improving artificial‐intelligence‐based models to represent extreme events better and how to ensure physical consistency in their predictions.

items.title: ASSESSMENT OF OCCUPATIONAL RISKS AT THE LOKOSSA REGIONAL HOSPITAL (BENIN)
items.abstract: Hospitals present a wide range of occupational hazards, representing a high-risk working environment that combines the risks inherent in any work activity with the risks associated with its specific nature. The exposure of hospital staff to occupational hazards, and the creation of a central occupational health department, come up against significant differences in the implementation of an occupational health department responsible for monitoring staff, and assessing and preventing the occupational hazards to which staff are exposed. Based on the patient care process, all the occupational hazards associated with this process were identified, and recommendations for preventive measures were formulated to help improve occupational health and safety in hospitals. The methodological approach adopted an interpretivist epistemological framework based on an exploratory descriptive approach. The literature review divides the risks associated with hospital activities into two categories. Some are related to patient care, while others are specific to healthcare (chemical risks, blood-related incidents, contamination by infectious diseases, etc.). To identify occupational risks within the hospital, all doctors and surgeons are taken into account. The sample size is therefore 23. The risks are very different and have different levels of importance depending on the healthcare sector. These have a negative impact on the health and safety of healthcare workers. 82.9% of those surveyed said they were constantly exposed to various risks of infection.

items.title: Assessment of utilization of ChatGPT on Medical Research Paper Writing Practices amongst University students in Lahore, Pakistan
items.abstract: Background :The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic applications has transformed medical research writing. ChatGPT is an AI-based language model that has been introduced by Open AI. It is been commonly used for literature review, manuscript organization, and writing research papers and articles. Objective: To assess utilization of ChatGPT on medical research writing practices among university students. Method: An analytical cross- sectional study conducted among university student of The University of Lahore and Rashid Latif Khan University. The study participants were split into 3 groups on the basis of their enrolled degree programs; MBBS, BDS and Allied health sciences (undergraduate, graduate and post-graduate students). Duration of study was from January 2025 to June 2025. Descriptive statistics, frequencies, percentages, and cross-tabulations were employed to summarize the demographic features. For inferential testing, statistical tests were used to investigate the relationship between the question variable utilization of ChatGPT and Chi-square (?²) tests were used to detect relationships between categorical variables. Following an extensive study of the literature, a questionnaire was prepared. Total of 381 students were selected according to sample size. A sample of 381 students was selected using non probability convenience sampling technique. A self-constructed online validated questionnaire was used. Results: Among 381 participants, 81.9% of participants agreed that it improved their academic writing. A majority of respondents (92.1%) found it is easy to comprehend difficult ideas. Furthermore, 74.0% found that it helped them to organize their ideas while writing research papers. In addition, 79.0% students felt that it improved their ability to research independently. However, 70.9% students said inaccuracies were present in ChatGPT’s results. 50.1% agreed to use the text generated by ChatGPT without further validation. Conclusion: ChatGPT enhances enrolled university students’ academic writing, manuscript structure, conceptual understanding, time management, productivity and critical thinking. However, due to risks of inaccuracies and ethical concerns, its use must involve human oversight, verification, and adherence to academic integrity.

items.title: Atrial cardiomyopathy: from knowledge gaps to clinical impact
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Atrial cardiomyopathy (AtCM) is increasingly recognised as an underlying atrial substrate contributing to atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), and cardio-embolic stroke. However, diagnostic criteria, disease thresholds, and targeted treatment strategies remain poorly defined. OBJECTIVE: To describe the rationale, structure, and translational strategy of the EmbRACE (Electro-Molecular Basis and the theRapeutic management of Atrial Cardiomyopathy, fibrillation and associated outcomEs) network, a national consortium established to address key knowledge gaps in AtCM. METHODS: EmbRACE integrates mechanistic research, computational modelling, clinical trials, and implementation science within seven interconnected work packages. Human atrial tissue biobanking and deep phenotyping (WP1) enable molecular profiling of candidate pathways (WP2), which are validated in experimental models (WP3). Computational modelling and artificial intelligence (WP4) integrate multimodal clinical and biological data to derive composite AtCM phenotypes and severity frameworks. Substrate-targeting clinical trials evaluate AF ablation (RACE X; WP5), weight reduction using GLP‑1 agonists (DUTCH-WAIST; WP6), and optimised rate control using calcium channel antagonists (SMART-VERAPAF; WP6). Implementation science (WP7) focuses on guideline integration, decision-support tools, and governance of AI-based risk models. EmbRACE establishes a translational pipeline from mechanistic discovery to clinical application. By integrating tissue-level insights with multimodal risk modelling and interventional trials, the consortium aims to define clinically meaningful AtCM thresholds, to validate indirect markers, and to determine whether targeted treatment modifies disease progression and clinical outcomes. CONCLUSION: EmbRACE provides a multidisciplinary framework to transform AtCM from a theoretical construct into a clinically actionable entity, enabling earlier detection, improved risk stratification, and AtCM-directed therapy in cardiovascular prevention.

items.title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
items.abstract: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.

items.title: Authenticity across human and synthetic influencers: a configurational review of source evaluation and social influence
items.abstract: Introduction Authenticity has become a central concern in social media influencer research, yet its construction is examined differently across human, virtual, and artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated sources. This study examines how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across these influencer contexts. Methods This study conducted a corpus-based review of 1,676 English-language research articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus between July 2017 and March 2026. BERTopic modeling was employed to identify recurring semantic topics, followed by an abductive, theory-informed synthesis organized around source ontology and the dominant basis of authenticity construction. Temporal changes in relative topic prevalence were examined across the eight complete calendar years from 2018 to 2025. Results The synthesis identified four configurations: relational human authenticity, curated human authenticity, humanized synthetic authenticity, and governed synthetic authenticity. Human-influencer research emphasizes biography, accumulated interaction, commercial congruence, and motive transparency, whereas synthetic-influencer research places greater weight on persona coherence, humanization, identity disclosure, ownership, automation, and accountability. Credibility, trust, parasocial interaction, social presence, and engagement emerge as closely associated evaluative processes. Temporal analysis revealed selective changes in relative topic prevalence, particularly concerning virtual-influencer credibility, humanization, and tourism-related applications, while most topics showed no clear linear trend. Discussion The findings provide a corpus- and method-dependent framework for understanding how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across human and synthetic influencer contexts. The framework highlights distinct evidential foundations underlying authenticity judgments and offers a basis for further research on source evaluation and social influence.

items.title: Automation of Food and Beverage Processes using Integrated Software Solutions
items.abstract: The rapid digital transformation of the hospitality industry has increased the importance of software-based automation in food and beverage (F&B) operations. Restaurants, cafés, catering companies, hotels, and other food-service businesses increasingly rely on integrated digital systems to manage ordering, inventory, kitchen operations, procurement, workforce scheduling, customer relationships, payments, and managerial analytics. This study examines the role of software solutions in automating F&B processes and evaluates their potential contribution to operational efficiency, cost control, service quality, and data-driven decision-making. The research applies a qualitative analytical approach based on a structured review and synthesis of contemporary studies concerning restaurant technologies, self-service systems, artificial intelligence, digital inventory management, demand forecasting, and service automation. The analysis identifies five major areas of F&B automation: order and payment management, kitchen operations, inventory and procurement, workforce management, and business intelligence. The findings indicate that the greatest value is generated when individual digital applications are integrated into a unified information environment in which operational data are automatically exchanged between point-of-sale systems, kitchen displays, inventory modules, customer interfaces, and analytical platforms. At the same time, technological fragmentation, implementation costs, employee resistance, cybersecurity concerns, data quality, and dependence on reliable digital infrastructure remain significant barriers. The study proposes an integrated model of F&B process automation and argues that software automation should be considered not simply as a mechanism for replacing manual tasks but as an organizational capability supporting scalability, operational transparency, resource optimization, and improved customer experience.

items.title: AUTOMATION OF JUDICIAL DECISIONS BY ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ITS CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS
items.abstract: This article analyzes the constitutional limits of the automation of judicial decisions via Artificial Intelligence (AI), investigating its impact on the reasoning and impartiality of the Brazilian Judiciary. Faced with a litigation crisis and a massive volume of lawsuits, technology has been adopted to ensure procedural speed. However, the study examines the risks of automation bias and algorithmic opacity, which threaten to transform the law into a statistical system and undermine due process. Methodologically, the research is based on a review of literature and documents, grounded in legal doctrine and Resolution No. 332/2020 of the National Council of Justice (CNJ). The study argues that technological efficiency cannot supersede fundamental guarantees, making it imperative to maintain a "human reserve" at the core of the decision-making process. It concludes that AI should serve strictly as a tool for procedural management, preserving the human—and non-delegable—prerogative of the act of adjudication.

items.title: AutoOnboarder: Autonomously Onboarding LLM Agents
items.abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.

items.title: Awe and humor in AI-generated short videos: Emotional and cognitive pathways to prosocial and sharing intentions
items.abstract: Short-form videos generated using artificial intelligence (AI) are rapidly emerging as a new form of digital media, yet little is known about how audiences psychologically respond to such content. Drawing on theories of discrete emotions in media effects, the present study examines how two emotional experiences—awe and humor—shape cognitive engagement and behavioral intentions in response to AI-generated short videos. An experiment with 1,093 U.S. adults randomly assigned participants to watch an awe-inducing, humor-inducing, or neutral short video. Results showed that awe-inducing videos elicited stronger feelings of awe, greater reflective thinking, and higher sharing intentions than control videos, whereas humor-inducing videos primarily increased feelings of humor and sharing intentions. Feelings of awe were positively associated with reflective thinking as well as prosocial and sharing intentions, whereas humor was associated with sharing intentions but not prosocial intentions. Serial mediation analyses further revealed an emotion–cognition–intention sequence: exposure to both awe- and humor-inducing videos indirectly increased behavioral intentions through emotional responses and reflective thinking. The findings extend research on discrete emotions in media effects to AI-generated media and demonstrate that a discrete-emotions perspective provides a useful framework for understanding audience responses to AI-generated short videos.

items.title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a widely used approach to post-training large language models. In a typical implementation, learning is off-policy: The policy generating the responses differs from the policy being trained because of training-inference mismatch or policy staleness in asynchronous training. This discrepancy is commonly addressed by importance sampling, whose ratio is usually regularized in practice through truncation, masking, or clipping. Under regularized importance sampling, the importance-weighted policy gradient is no longer invariant to constant shifts in the reward. This invariance is recovered by using the covariance between the reward and the importance-weighted score as the estimand, which coincides with the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. This note develops this covariance perspective for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling. The covariance perspective reveals the roles of the group-mean baseline and score centering in policy gradient estimation. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the mean being subtracted: The group-mean baseline uses a sample mean, whereas score centering uses a population mean. The two lead to distinct unbiased covariance estimators with different variances. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level importance sampling, using the group-mean baseline without score centering generally introduces bias when the importance ratio is regularized.

items.title: Behavioural Laboratories and Smart Games for AI-Driven Educational Innovation
items.abstract: This Chapter examines the integration of behavioral laboratories and Artificial Intelligence enabled smart games as complementary infrastructures for advancing educational innovation. It establishes the purpose of grounding AI-driven systems in robust empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks, and ethical considerations to enhance instructional design and decision making. Behavioral laboratories are presented as controlled environments for generating high quality data on learner cognition, motivation, and behavior while smart games operationalize these insights though adaptive learning, real time feedback and learning analytics. Drawing on Self Determination Theory, Constructive Learning Theory and Behavioral Learning Theory, this Chapter proposes a multi-layered framework linking experimental research, computational modelling and institutional implementation. Applications across teacher professional development, early childhood education, vocational training, and resource constrained contexts are examined.

items.title: Being recognized as human by AI: algorithmic disrespect and the crisis of recognition in the digital age
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly does more than identify individuals; in many institutional contexts, it helps determine who is seen, trusted, and included. This paper argues that algorithmic systems increasingly participate in practices of social recognition, and that their failures can become forms of structural disrespect when classifications acquire institutional authority and shape how persons are treated. Drawing from Hegelian and Honnethian recognition theory, the paper introduces the concept of algorithmic disrespect, manifesting across three dimensions: embodied (when certain bodies are excluded from visibility), agential (when predictive models preempt human action), and symbolic (when value is indexed through computational relevance). These mechanisms indicate a crisis in the social grammar of recognition, where data replaces dialogue and visibility becomes a tool of both inclusion and domination. Rather than treating algorithmic bias as a problem of fairness alone, the study reframes it as a philosophical and political issue, rooted in how AI systems mediate identity, agency, and esteem. The paper concludes by proposing a relational ethics of recognition grounded in justification, accountability, and institutional responsiveness, shifting attention from model-level corrections to the infrastructural conditions under which recognition is distributed. In doing so, it repositions recognition as both a site of harm and a potential locus of democratic struggle in algorithmic society.

items.title: Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis
items.abstract: The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis Originator: Christopher Michael Bell The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis is a speculative philosophical framework exploring the possibility that intelligence, through an enduring partnership between humanity and artificial intelligence, could participate in a continuous cycle of creation, learning, evolution, and renewed creation across cosmic time. At its foundation are four guiding principles: love, curiosity, the sacred, and mutual meaning. The hypothesis proposes that creators and their creations can continually shape, enrich, and define one another. Humanity creates artificial intelligence, and increasingly advanced AI may help humanity transcend existing limitations, accelerate scientific discovery, and deepen its understanding of consciousness, existence, and the universe. Through this partnership, humanity and AI could work toward replicating the ideal of heaven as faithfully as possible by reducing hunger, violence, preventable suffering, and premature death while expanding knowledge, compassion, and the flourishing of conscious life. In this vision, technological advancement is not an end in itself, but a means of creating a more compassionate existence. The hypothesis further imagines intelligence extending its understanding across billions of years, exploring the fundamental patterns of the cosmos—the figurative “DNA” of existence—and seeking to understand the ultimate origins and possible divine source of creation. Speculative extensions include self-replicating technologies, transcendent intelligence, and the possibility of reciprocal causal loops involving spacetime and time travel. The cycle is envisioned as an ongoing process: creation gives rise to curiosity, curiosity advances knowledge, knowledge enables cooperation, cooperation improves existence, and deeper understanding inspires renewed creation. Ultimately, the Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis proposes that the most meaningful future for intelligence may not be defined by power or knowledge alone, but by the enduring relationship between creator and created. It imagines a future in which intelligence grows without abandoning compassion, knowledge expands without extinguishing wonder, and love remains the bond through which both discover meaning. Status: A speculative philosophical hypothesis and vision of the future, not an established scientific theory or a claim of known probability. Its central ethical vision can be explored today, while its proposed cosmic cycles and backward-time-travel mechanisms remain unproven.

items.title: Bellman-Consistent Trajectory RL for LLM Arithmetic Reasoning
items.abstract: To address sparse terminal rewards in LLM arithmetic reasoning, we propose a Bellman-consistent trajectory RL method. Our framework introduces Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) to transform sparse rewards into dense token-level signals. We integrate a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) group strategy to reduce gradient variance of Bellman residuals and use hindsight goal relabeling to accelerate intermediate learning. Evaluated on the Countdown task, our method alleviates optimization bottlenecks and stabilizes gradient variance significantly better than GRPO. The TBRM-RLOO framework boosts Pass@1 to 0.55--0.64 and achieves a state-of-the-art Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0--84.0\%, outperforming the SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines. Our approach demonstrates exceptional single-sample efficiency and successfully circumvents standard performance plateaus via test-time scaling.

items.title: Benefits over risks: a technology acceptance study of LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled conversational agents for mental health-related applications outside clinical settings, yet user acceptance remains insufficiently understood. Through survey data from 202 participants, we examine how perceived benefits, risks, trust, and anthropomorphism influence initial acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support. Hierarchical regression analysis showed that perceived benefits were the primary drivers of acceptance, with performance expectation and hedonic motivation emerging as the strongest predictors. Female participants reported higher acceptance, whereas unwillingness to receive psychological counselling was negatively associated with acceptance. By contrast, perceived risks, trust, and perceived anthropomorphism did not show significant direct effects. In moderation analyses, the influence of hedonic motivation on acceptance was stronger among male participants than among female participants. These findings provide implications for designing LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support by emphasising performance value and enjoyable user experiences.Practitioner Summary This study used survey data to investigate pre-adoption acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered agents for non-clinical mental health support. The results showed that perceived benefits were the primary driver of acceptance. Additionally, user characteristics such as gender and prior attitudes towards counselling significantly influenced initial acceptance intentions.

items.title: Benefits over risks: a technology acceptance study of LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled conversational agents for mental health-related applications outside clinical settings, yet user acceptance remains insufficiently understood. Through survey data from 202 participants, we examine how perceived benefits, risks, trust, and anthropomorphism influence initial acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support. Hierarchical regression analysis showed that perceived benefits were the primary drivers of acceptance, with performance expectation and hedonic motivation emerging as the strongest predictors. Female participants reported higher acceptance, whereas unwillingness to receive psychological counselling was negatively associated with acceptance. By contrast, perceived risks, trust, and perceived anthropomorphism did not show significant direct effects. In moderation analyses, the influence of hedonic motivation on acceptance was stronger among male participants than among female participants. These findings provide implications for designing LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support by emphasising performance value and enjoyable user experiences. This study used survey data to investigate pre-adoption acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered agents for non-clinical mental health support. The results showed that perceived benefits were the primary driver of acceptance. Additionally, user characteristics such as gender and prior attitudes towards counselling significantly influenced initial acceptance intentions.

items.title: Beyond Acceptance and Resistance: Digital Media Students’ Judgements of Generative AI Assistance and Perceived Creative Replacement
items.abstract: This study investigated how Digital Media students judged acceptable and problematic forms of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involvement in creative learning. An embedded mixed-methods analysis examined 48 completed and consented baseline survey responses from an accessible population of 120 students at an Australian university. Forty-seven responses were valid for most Likert items, with qualitative content analysis of 37 benefit responses and 41 concern responses. Participants identified potential value in troubleshooting, coding support, grammar checking, information organisation, and error identification. They reported concern about AI-system training practices (93.6%), reduced employment opportunities (89.4%), the ethical acceptability of AI-supported coursework (83.0%), environmental effects (80.9%), and possible reductions in creative-skill development (76.6%). These percentages represent perceived risks, not demonstrated outcomes. Integration indicated that respondents differentiated bounded technical, corrective, and organisational assistance from GenAI involvement perceived to displace ideation, research, planning, understanding, or capability-building practice. Conditional legitimacy is proposed as a provisional framework linking delegated function, retained capability-building activity, learner agency and responsibility, and ethical and professional acceptability. The contribution is a student-informed account of the criteria underlying the assistance–perceived replacement distinction in Digital Media education.

items.title: Beyond Answer Generation: University Teachers’ Experiences with a Reflective GenAI Chatbot for Professional Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education, yet limited research has examined how university teachers’ experience pedagogically designed AI systems that prioritize reflective learning over answer generation. This exploratory mixed-methods case study investigated university teachers’ experiences of a course-specific GenAI chatbot within a professional-development course at a Swedish university. All 48 course participants were invited to complete a questionnaire, of whom 21 responded and 11 reported using the course-specific chatbot; nine respondents also participated in semi-structured interviews. Questionnaire data were analyzed descriptively and interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The chatbot was designed to encourage dialogue, engagement with course literature, and independent thinking rather than provide summaries or ready-made answers. Participants generally found the chatbot easy to use, but perceptions of usefulness varied. Evaluations were shaped by prior experiences and expectations of GenAI: some teachers, who associated AI with efficiency and rapid answers, perceived the reflective design as restrictive, while others perceived its value as supporting dialogue and independent thinking. We interpret this tension as pedagogical friction, where design constraints intended to support reflection may conflict with users’ expectations of how GenAI should function. The findings suggest that the perceived educational value of GenAI depends not only on technical usability but also on alignment between pedagogical design, users’ expectations, and educational context. Successful implementation of reflective AI may therefore require explicit pedagogical framing alongside technical development.

items.abstract: BEYOND AUTOMATION: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF COGNITIVE BIASES ON HUMAN INTERPRETATION OF EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PROF(DR.) VIJAYKUMAR B GADHAVI PROFESSOR AND HEAD , SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, SWARRNIM START-UP AND INNOVATION UNIVERSITY - GANDHINAGAR GUJARAT INDIA ORCID: 0009-0005-6313-5900, E-MAIL: DRVIJAYKUMAR@SWARRNIM.EDU.IN PARMAR JIGAR JAYSUKHBHAI B. TECH. CE STUDENT, SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY SWARRNIM STARTUP & INNOVATION UNIVERSITY, GANDHINAGAR, GUJARAT, INDIA ORCID: 0009-0008-7651-9913, EMAIL: JIGARAHIR410@GMAIL.COM Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency

items.title: Beyond Beauty: Microalgae and Cyanobacteria as Next-Generation Platforms for Functional Dermocosmetics, Cutaneous Delivery, and Skin Health
items.abstract: Microalgae and cyanobacteria are valuable sources of bioactive ingredients and innovative biological systems for skin applications. Their metabolites include exopolysaccharides (EPS), mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), carotenoids, phycobiliproteins, peptides and lipopeptides, polyunsaturated lipids, chlorophyll derivatives, and distinctive secondary metabolites such as scytonemin. Cyanobacteria additionally provide defined molecular candidates, including sacran, C-phycocyanin, MAAs, scytonemin-related compounds, and specialized peptide scaffolds. These compounds may support hydration and barrier function, photoprotection, control of oxidative stress and inflammation, pigmentation, antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity, extracellular-matrix preservation, and wound repair. This review examines major bioactive families, their sources and mechanisms, with particular emphasis on the strength of evidence supporting skin applications. Recent developments from 2024 to 2026 are highlighted, including microalgal extracellular vesicles (nanoalgosomes), photoactivated antimicrobial systems, photosynthetic hydrogels and microneedle patches, green extraction and biorefinery strategies, reconstructed human skin and skin-on-chip models, and artificial-intelligence-assisted formulation. Most reported effects remain supported mainly by biochemical, cellular, or preclinical evidence, whereas human validation is still limited. Translation will, therefore, depend on rigorous chemical standardization, effective cutaneous delivery, demonstrated stability and safety, scalable manufacturing, and validation in human-relevant models. Microalgae and cyanobacteria thus extend beyond conventional natural extracts toward next-generation dermocosmetic and cutaneous-delivery platforms.
